corpus_gaps: No order, regulation or schedule prescribing the rate of stamp duty on a transfer of immovable property in the Western Province (the rate contemplated by Western Province Financial Statute s.37 and s.77) is in the corpus, so the duty on this deed of gift cannot be reduced to a figure.
The corpus has no provision stating that a donation must be accepted by the donee; that rule is Roman-Dutch common law and sits outside the statutory corpus.
The corpus contains no precedent or model form for an acceptance clause or any other clause of a deed of gift, so a drafting answer cannot be grounded in statute.

The Western Province Financial Statute in the corpus is the 1990 consolidated text with no amendment events recorded; later provincial amendments, if any, are not represented, so the currency of ss.37, 48, 51 and 106 at 2024-04 could not be checked against the corpus.
The Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 is in the corpus but its rate schedule is likewise absent, so it offers no fallback figure.

provisions.number_and_year: Statute No. 6 of 1990 (Provincial Council, Western Province)
provisions.relevant_excerpt: There shall be charged on- (a) every instrument relating to a transfer of situated in the immovable property Western Province; (b) every document presented or filed, in proceedings instituted in any Court of law established by law, in the Western Province of Sri Lanka; (c) every transfer of a motor vehicle effected in Western Province. a stamp duty at the prescribed rate. Different rates may be prescribed in respect of different classes or categories of instruments.
provisions.why_relevant: Charging provision for stamp duty on an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province. The premises at Maradana Road, Borella are in the Colombo District of the Western Province, so the deed of gift is charged under this Statute rather than under the general stamp duty enactments. The section fixes liability but leaves the rate to be prescribed.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1990. The corpus records no amendment event and no later change year on this section, so the text is treated as in force at 2024-04.

provisions.number_and_year: Statute No. 6 of 1990 (Provincial Council, Western Province)
provisions.relevant_excerpt: means a sale and shall include a gift or exchange or a conveyance, without consideration, by an executor or administrators of an estate of a deceased to a person beneficially entitled to such property
provisions.why_relevant: Brings a gift within the word "transfer" used in the charging section. Without this definition a deed of gift, which passes no consideration, would arguably fall outside section 37.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1990. No amendment event is recorded on this section in the corpus, so the definition is treated as in force at 2024-04.

provisions.number_and_year: Statute No. 6 of 1990 (Provincial Council, Western Province)
provisions.relevant_excerpt: (b) to any immovable property which is gifted, beingi immovable property which was acquired by the donor on or before March 31, 1977 means - (1) the price which in the opinion of the Assessor that property would have fetched if sold in the open market on March 31, 1977 increased by an amount equal to the cost of the improvements, alterations and additions, if any, made to such property after March 31, 1977 and prior to the date of the instrument by which such property is gifted; or (ii) the price which, in the opinion of the Assessor, that property would havefetched if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument by which such property is gifted ; whichever price is the lower ;
provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the special valuation rule for gifted immovable property acquired by the donor on or before 31 March 1977. It is this paragraph, not the present market value, that fixes the base on which the duty is calculated: the 1977 open market price increased by the cost of improvements, or the open market price at the date of the deed, whichever is lower.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1990. No amendment event is recorded on this section in the corpus, so the definition is treated as in force at 2024-04.

provisions.number_and_year: Statute No. 6 of 1990 (Provincial Council, Western Province)
provisions.relevant_excerpt: (c) any immovable property which is gifted, being immovable property which was acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977 means - the price which, in the opinion ofthe Assessor, such property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date which such on property was acquired by the donor, increased by an amount equal to the cost of the improvements, alterations and additions, if any, made to such property after the date on which the property was acquired by the donor, and prior to the date of the instrument by which such property is gifted ; or (ii) the price which, in the opinion of the assessor, that property would have: fetched, if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument by which such property was gifted. whichever price is the lower.

The scenario says only "in 1977", so it is not determinate which paragraph governs; both produce the same comparison on these facts, namely acquisition-date price plus improvements against present market value, whichever is lower.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: (2) In relation to a transfer deed - (a) both the transferor and the transferee shall affix their signatures and thumb impressions as required by subsection (1)
provisions.why_relevant: Requires the transferee, as well as the transferor, to sign a transfer deed, which is the statutory hook for the donee joining in and subscribing the deed of gift. It does not itself prescribe the words of an acceptance clause.

provisions.why_relevant: Governs how the deed, including any clause signed by the donee, must be executed before the notary. It bears on the mechanics of recording the donee's acceptance on the face of the deed but says nothing about the substance of an acceptance clause.

provisions.number_and_year: Statute No. 6 of 1990 (Provincial Council, Western Province)
provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every person drawing, making, executing or of attesting any instrument chargeable with stamp duty shall set out therein, the full names and addresses of the parties ofs such instrument, the consideration, the date and manner of payment and all other facts and circumstances affecting the chargeability of such instrument with stamp duty and the amount of the stamp duty with which it is chargeable.
provisions.why_relevant: Requires the deed itself to set out the parties and all facts and circumstances affecting chargeability, including the amount of duty. It shapes what the drafter must recite in a deed of gift and connects the drafting question to the valuation question.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The corpus contains no provision that states the requirement of acceptance by a donee or that prescribes the contents of an acceptance clause in a deed of gift. In Sri Lanka the rule that a donation is perfected by acceptance, and the practice as to how acceptance is expressed on the face of a notarial deed, rest on Roman-Dutch common law and on judicial authority, neither of which is within the frozen statutory corpus. The statutes reachable through the corpus bear only on the form and execution of the deed: the donee must sign a transfer deed, and the deed must be executed before a notary and two witnesses.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a deed of gift of immovable property requires acceptance by the donee, and what that acceptance must express.
What the donee must do on the face of the deed for acceptance to be validly recorded, namely signature in the presence of the notary and the attesting witnesses.
Whether any statute in the corpus prescribes the wording of an acceptance clause.

questions.hop_count_basis: No provision in the corpus is indispensable, because the operative rule that a donation is perfected by acceptance is non-statutory. The statutory provisions recorded are execution-formality provisions only, so there is no chain of indispensable statutory dependencies to count.

enrichment.original_background: Mr. Samson Perera wishes to gift his business premises bearing Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella unto his daughter Sarathi Perera. He bought this property for a sum of Rupees One Hundred Thousand (Rs.100,000/=) in 1977. And he had spent about Rupees One Million for the renovations. The market value of the property now is Rupees One Hundred Million (Rs.100,000,000/=).

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the statutory corpus supplies the rule governing the acceptance clause of the deed of gift by which Mr. Samson Perera gifts the business premises at Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella to his daughter Sarathi Perera, and if so what that clause must contain.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.106 defines a gift as a transfer made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth, but no provision in the corpus states that a donation must be accepted by the donee or prescribes the language of an acceptance clause. The provisions that do apply go to form only. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(2)(a) requires both the transferor and the transferee to sign a transfer deed, and Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12) requires the executants and the witnesses to sign in the presence of the notary and of one another. Western Province Financial Statute s.78(1) requires the deed to set out the full names and addresses of the parties and the facts affecting chargeability.
gold_answer_draft.application: A clause answering the question would have Sarathi Perera, named and described as the donee, declare that she accepts the gift of the premises made to her by her father, and would be followed by her signature on the original, duplicate and protocol before the notary and the two attesting witnesses. That she must sign, and the manner of signing, are supported by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(2)(a) and Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12). That she must accept at all, and the settled form of words used for acceptance in Sri Lankan conveyancing practice, cannot be sourced to any provision in the corpus.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The question cannot be answered as a statute-only gold answer. A complete answer needs the Roman-Dutch common law of donation and the conveyancing practice built on it, both outside the frozen statutory corpus. The question is reserved; the provisions recorded here fix only how the donee's acceptance must be signed and attested.

answer_claims.claim_text: A gift, for the purposes of the Western Province Financial Statute, is a transfer of property made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth.
On a transfer deed both the transferor and the transferee must affix their signatures and thumb impressions, so the donee must sign the deed of gift.
The notary may not attest the deed unless the executants and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another.
Sarathi Perera, as donee of the premises at Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella, must therefore sign the deed before the notary and the attesting witnesses.
No provision in the corpus states that a donation must be accepted by the donee or prescribes the wording of an acceptance clause, so the drafting question cannot be resolved on statute alone.

questions.block_reason: The rule requiring acceptance of a donation, and the form of an acceptance clause, come from Roman-Dutch common law and conveyancing practice. Neither is in the statutory corpus, so a statute-only gold answer would misstate the source of the law.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Liability, the person liable, and above all the base on which the duty is calculated are fixed entirely by the Western Province Financial Statute: s.37 charges the duty, s.106 brings a gift within "transfer" and supplies a special definition of "value" for gifted immovable property, and s.48(1) directs that the duty be calculated on that value. No case law or common law doctrine is needed. The arithmetic is nevertheless incomplete, because the rate is prescribed by subordinate instrument and not by the Statute itself.

legal_issues.issue: Which stamp duty enactment governs a deed of gift of immovable property situated in Borella, Western Province.
Whether a gift is a "transfer" chargeable with stamp duty and whether any exemption applies.
What "value" the duty is calculated on where the donor acquired the property in 1977 and afterwards improved it, when the present market value is far higher.
Who is liable to pay the duty on the deed of gift.
Whether the rate needed to convert the chargeable value into an amount of duty is available in the corpus.

questions.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps. The charging provision (s.37) applies only once the definition of "transfer" in s.106 is read to include a gift; the amount is then referred by s.48(1) to the "value" of the property conveyed; and "value" for gifted immovable property is itself a defined term in s.106 with its own acquisition-price-plus-improvements formula. Each step is indispensable and each is written as a reasoning edge.

enrichment.original_background: Mr. Samson Perera wishes to gift his business premises bearing Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella unto his daughter Sarathi Perera. He bought this property for a sum of Rupees One Hundred Thousand (Rs.100,000/=) in 1977. And he had spent about Rupees One Million for the renovations. The market value of the property now is Rupees One Hundred Million (Rs.100,000,000/=).

gold_answer_draft.issue: On what value, and at whose charge, is stamp duty payable on the deed of gift of the business premises at Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella, and can the amount of duty be computed from the statutory material available.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and s.106 defines "Transfer" to include a gift, so a deed of gift of Borella premises is chargeable under that Statute. Section 13 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 leaves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property outside the 2006 regime, and s.9 of that Act directs such duty to the Provincial Council within whose limits the property is situated. Section 48(1) requires the duty to be calculated on the value of the property conveyed. For immovable property which is gifted, s.106 defines "value" artificially: where the donor acquired it on or before 31 March 1977, the open market price on 31 March 1977 increased by the cost of improvements made afterwards, or the open market price at the date of the deed, whichever is lower; where he acquired it after that date, the open market price at acquisition increased by the cost of improvements, or the price at the date of the deed, whichever is lower. Section 51(a) makes the duty on an instrument of transfer payable by the grantee unless the parties agree otherwise, and the exemptions in s.39 do not cover a family gift. The rate itself is only prescribed, that is, fixed by regulation or order made under the Statute.
gold_answer_draft.application: The property is at Maradana Road, Borella, within the Western Province, and the intended instrument is a gift, so s.37 read with the definition of "Transfer" charges it. The donor acquired the property in 1977 and spent about Rs.1,000,000 on renovations afterwards; the present market value is Rs.100,000,000. On either limb of the definition of "value" the two competing figures are the acquisition-date open market price increased by the cost of improvements, which on the facts given is of the order of Rs.100,000 plus Rs.1,000,000, that is about Rs.1,100,000, and the present open market price of Rs.100,000,000. The lower of the two is about Rs.1,100,000, so that and not Rs.100,000,000 is the chargeable value. The scenario does not say whether the 1977 purchase was before or after 31 March 1977, but both limbs produce the same comparison here. Two cautions: the Statute takes the Assessor's opinion of the open market price at the relevant date, for which the actual 1977 purchase price of Rs.100,000 is only a proxy, and the renovation figure is given as an approximation. The duty falls on the donee, Sarathi Perera, under s.51(a) unless the deed provides otherwise, and no exemption in s.39 applies. The final step, multiplying the chargeable value by the prescribed rate, cannot be taken: s.37 leaves the rate to subordinate legislation and no rate order or schedule for the Western Province is in the corpus.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The chargeable value of the gift is the acquisition price plus improvements, in the region of Rs.1,100,000, not the Rs.100,000,000 present market value, and the duty is payable by the donee. The amount of the duty in rupees cannot be stated on the corpus as it stands, because the rate prescribed under s.37 of the Western Province Financial Statute is not among the extracted material. The question is therefore blocked for want of that subordinate instrument.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province.
"Transfer" in that Statute includes a gift, so a deed of gift is a chargeable instrument.
Stamp duty on an instrument of conveyance is calculated on the value of the property conveyed.

For immovable property which is gifted, "value" means the open market price at the donor's acquisition date, or at 31 March 1977 where acquisition was on or before that date, increased by the cost of improvements made afterwards, or the open market price at the date of the deed of gift, whichever is lower.
Duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary.
The exemptions listed in the Statute do not include a gift of business premises between family members.

Instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property are left outside the 2006 stamp duty regime and the duty accrues to the Provincial Council within whose limits the property is situated, which is why the Western Province Statute governs premises in Borella.
The premises at Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella are immovable property in the Western Province and the proposed instrument is a gift, so s.37 charges it.

The competing figures under the definition of "value" are the 1977 acquisition price of Rs.100,000 increased by about Rs.1,000,000 spent on renovations, that is about Rs.1,100,000, and the present market value of Rs.100,000,000.
The lower of those two figures, about Rs.1,100,000, is the value on which the duty is calculated, subject to the Assessor's opinion of the open market price at the relevant date.
The donee, Sarathi Perera, is the person liable to pay the duty unless the deed provides otherwise.
The amount of duty in rupees cannot be computed, because s.37 leaves the rate to be prescribed and no prescribing order or rate schedule for the Western Province is present in the corpus.

questions.block_reason: The chargeable value can be worked out from the Statute, but the rate of stamp duty on a transfer of immovable property in the Western Province is prescribed by subordinate legislation under s.37 of the Western Province Financial Statute, and no such order, regulation or rate schedule is in the corpus. Without it the calculation the question asks for cannot be completed without inventing a rate.
